newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish honours nationalist "bad boy" at funeral.
newsitem.headline: Turkish honours nationalist "bad boy" at funeral.

text.p: The Turkish capital ground to a halt on Tuesday to honour Alparslan Turkes, an ultra-nationalist "bad boy" whose vision of Turkic unity from the Balkans to the Great Wall of China has entered the political mainstream.

"Condolences to his family and friends, to the Turkic world, the political community and our nation," Turkey's highest religious official, Mehmet Nuri Yilmaz, said at a funeral ceremony in Ankara's main Kocatepe mosque.

In a clear sign of political rehabilitation, former political rivals President Suleyman Demirel and Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan were among tens of thousands of mourners who stood in the mosque's courtyard in driving snow.
Police closed much of the city centre to traffic to allow huge crowds of supporters chanting "Turkes is the Basbug (Chieftain)" to march through the streets.
Followers, known as "Grey Wolves", carried red-and-white Turkish flags, the three-crescent standard of his Nationalist Action Party and the colours of the Turkic states in Central Asia.

Turkes, who died of a heart attack on Saturday aged 80, campaigned to unite Turkic nations. "He was the leader of all Turks as far as Eastern Turkestan," said supporter Adem Guler, carrying a banner with a wolf ringed by the Islamic crescent.
"It's a great loss for all of us."
Turkic-speaking Uighurs took part in separatist riots in February in western China's Xinjiang region, known to many Turks as East Turkestan.
Ethnic Turks from Germany, Cyprus, Bulgaria, Crimea and Central Asia attended the funeral, which began with a minute's silence by MPs at the parliament building.

The Cyprus-born Turkes had a love-hate relationship with the political establishment. As an army colonel, he played a leading role in a coup in 1960 but soon fell out with fellow officers and was given a foreign posting to keep him out of harm's way.

His Grey Wolves fought leftists in street battles in the late 1970s in which more than 5,000 people died. The violence helped prompt the army to launch another coup and send Turkes to a military jail for four and a half years.
His nationalist views have a powerful hold in Turkish public life despite Turkes's failing in 1995 to win the 10 percent of the vote needed to capture any seats in parliament under election laws.
Larger conservative parties have taken on many of his far-right ideas over the years.
His bid to bring the Turkic nations together, previously scoffed at by many Turks as fantasy, gained credence after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

However, former Soviet Moslem republics like Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan still maintain close ties to Moscow and links to Turkey failed to live up to the expectations of pan-Turkic idealists such as Turkes.
In recent years, Turkes made his influence felt among the powerful security forces, particularly policemen and soldiers fighting Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebels in southeast Turkey.

"In the 1990s, Turkes saw that the country was in danger from the separatist PKK," the mass-circulation Sabah daily said in an editorial on Tuesday. "He was an important element in stopping backsliding by state officials," it said.
Turkes denied the existence of Turkey's estimated 10 million Kurds as a separate people and encouraged tough military methods against Kurdish activists.
